opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few distinct limits worth separating out.

The first is that returns to inference compute seem to be quite sensitive to the underlying model. If the base model doesn't have the relevant knowledge or the right capabilities to begin with, then letting it think longer, sample more, or search over more candidate solutions only gets you so far. You can't search your way to an answer the model has essentially no probability of generating. So inference compute and training compute look more like complements than substitutes. You need a reasonably strong model before extra thinking time pays off much.

The second is verification. A lot of the impressive gains from inference scaling come from domains where you can cheaply check whether an answer is right: math problems with known answers, code with unit tests, that kind of thing. There you can generate many attempts and pick the one that passes. In domains where verification is hard, like open-ended research, strategy, or writing, you don't have a clean signal to select on. You end up relying on the model's own judgment of its outputs, and that judgment is often the same thing that's limiting it in the first place.

Third, there are diminishing returns within a single chain of reasoning. Performance often goes up roughly with the log of compute spent, so each doubling buys you less. And past some point models can go in circles, second-guess correct answers, or accumulate errors over very long reasoning traces. Keeping coherent over very long horizons is itself a capability the model has to have learned.

Then there's the economic side. Inference compute is paid every time you run the model, whereas training compute is a one-time cost amortized over all your users. If you get a capability by spending a hundred times more at inference, that's a recurring cost. For many applications it's worth it, but it constrains how widely you can deploy that capability. It also matters for latency, since some tasks just can't wait for a model to think for an hour.

That said, I don't want to overstate these limits. A lot of the inference scaling we've seen is really about training models to use inference compute well, through reinforcement learning on reasoning. So the frontier keeps moving: as models get better at reasoning, verifying their own work, and staying on track over long horizons, the useful range of inference compute extends. My overall view is that it's a genuinely important new axis of scaling, but it's tied to progress in training and doesn't replace it.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe repeated chess games against Kasparov, switching sides, or replaying his moves.

r003.rationale: The response explains that when verification is hard, there is no clean signal for selecting among generated answers, limiting the gains from inference scaling.

r005.rationale: The response gives no tentative Epoch estimate or roughly hundredfold training-compute comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different limits, and it's worth separating them out, because they operate on different scales.

The first is just the empirical shape of the scaling curve. When you look at the work people have done on test-time compute, things like letting a model think for longer, sampling many solutions and picking the best one, running search over reasoning steps, you do get improvement, but it tends to be roughly logarithmic. You spend ten times more compute at inference and you get something like a constant increment in performance. That's actually the same qualitative shape as training compute scaling, so it's not that inference scaling is uniquely bad, but it does mean that getting a lot more capability out of inference compute alone requires enormous increases in spending per task. And there's a question of how far along that curve people will actually be willing to go. For a problem where the answer is extremely valuable, say a proof or a hard engineering design, you might be happy to spend thousands of dollars of compute. For most queries you're not.

The second limit is that inference-time compute mostly helps on tasks where you have some way of verifying or at least scoring candidate answers. Math, code, formal puzzles, things where you can check the output, those benefit a lot. Tasks where the quality of the answer is diffuse or subjective, writing, judgment calls, open-ended research taste, there the model doesn't have a clean signal to search against, and so spending more compute looks more like rephrasing the same answer in many ways. You can use the model itself as the verifier, and that helps to a degree, but then you're bounded by how good the model's own judgment is, and that's a property set at training time, not inference time.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that inference compute and training compute aren't really independent levers. A lot of the gains people attribute to inference-time scaling are really downstream of training the model to make good use of that extra compute. You have to teach it to reason in long chains, to backtrack, to check its own work. A base model that hasn't been trained that way just doesn't benefit much from being given more tokens. So the frontier is really set by how well you've trained the model to exploit inference compute, and that pushes you back toward training compute as the binding constraint. In the long run my expectation is that the two get traded off against each other, with labs picking whatever mix is cheapest for a given level of capability, and the ratio shifts around over time depending on things like hardware costs and how expensive deployment is relative to training.

And then the last limit is really an economic one. If you're deploying a model to a very large number of users, inference compute is a recurring cost per query, whereas training is a one-off. So you can't just push inference scaling arbitrarily far in a product setting, because the cost scales with usage. That's why I'd expect a lot of inference-time gains to eventually be distilled back into the weights, where you run expensive reasoning once, generate lots of high-quality data, and train a cheaper model to produce those answers directly. So inference scaling ends up being a mechanism for improving training rather than a substitute for it.

So the short version is: it works, the returns look log-linear, it's strongest where you can verify answers, and over the long run it mostly gets folded back into the training process rather than remaining a separate dimension.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that more time to think is only useful if the model has some productive way of using that time. You can generate more candidate answers, explore different approaches, or check your work. But you need some ability to distinguish a better answer from a worse one. Otherwise, you might just produce a longer, more elaborate mistake.

That makes this particularly promising in domains where verification is relatively easy. With programming, for example, you can run tests. With some mathematical problems, you can check a proposed solution. It's much less straightforward when you're asking for a judgment about the world and there's no readily available signal that tells you whether your reasoning is on track.

There's also diminishing returns. If a model keeps exploring very similar approaches, additional computation doesn't buy you much. And if it's missing some crucial information, thinking for longer won't necessarily supply that information. It might need to interact with the world or perform an experiment.

Then there are the practical constraints of cost and latency. You might be willing to let a system work for hours on a valuable scientific problem, but you probably wouldn't accept that for every conversational response. So I think inference-time compute is a substantial additional avenue for improving performance, but how far it takes you depends on the task and on whether the model has learned to use that computation effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the model has a useful way to spend that additional compute. You can’t simply let it run for longer and assume that its answers will keep getting better. It needs some procedure for exploring possible solutions, checking them, and deciding which ones to pursue.

That’s particularly promising in domains where you can verify an answer fairly cheaply. If you’re writing code, for example, you can run tests. In mathematics, you might be able to check a proof. You can generate lots of candidates and use that feedback to search for a good one. But for something like giving strategic advice, it’s much less clear how you determine whether the extra reasoning has actually improved the answer. The model might just produce a more elaborate version of the same mistake.

There’s also a limit from the capabilities of the underlying model. If it has essentially no chance of generating the right idea, sampling more answers may be very inefficient. And if its errors are correlated, you don’t get the same benefits you would from independent attempts.

So I’d expect substantial gains from inference-time compute, but with diminishing returns, and with quite a lot of variation across tasks. The practical constraint is also cost and latency: an improvement that requires hours of computation might be worthwhile for a scientific discovery, but much less useful for an everyday interaction.
